title: Collision and Broadcast Domains: The Complete Beginner's Guide

scenes.narration: An open plan office, or one with cubicles. Which one is quieter? Networks have the same question.

scenes.heading: Open plan or cubicles
scenes.narration: In an open plan office, everyone hears everyone. If two people speak at once, it's a collision. That's a collision domain, like a hub. A switch gives every person a cubicle, so each port is its own collision domain. But if someone shouts for everyone, the whole floor still hears. That's a broadcast, and the floor is a broadcast domain. Only a router, or a V L A N, builds walls between floors.

scenes.heading: What splits what
scenes.narration: Here's the key. A hub makes one collision domain for all ports. A switch makes one per port. A switch alone keeps one broadcast domain. A router, or a V L A N, makes a new one.

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three mix-ups. A switch doesn't make one big collision domain. It makes one for each port. V L A Ns split broadcast domains, not collision domains. And a router splits broadcast domains, while each of its interfaces is its own collision domain too.

items.wrong: A switch is one collision domain

items.right: They split broadcast; each interface is its own collision domain

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.cta: Try the Courseiva network domains lab
scenes.narration: So, to recap. Switch ports split collision domains. Routers and V L A Ns split broadcast domains. Count them: that's a favourite exam question. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva network domains lab.
